items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon: What can the light from a distant glowing nebula or a faraway galaxy tell astronomers about it?

body.html: Astronomers collect only light from the object. We need to say what properties of that light reveal information, and what each one tells us.

Light carries information in its wavelength (color) and its brightness. Spectral lines identify the elements, the Doppler shift 𝛥𝜆= ± (𝑣/ 𝑐)𝜆 gives the motion toward or away from us, and the inverse-square law 𝐸= 𝑃/ (4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>) links apparent brightness to distance.

(1) Each element emits or absorbs light only at particular wavelengths, so matching the pattern of lines to laboratory patterns tells us which elements are present. (2) If the whole pattern is shifted to longer wavelengths the object is moving away; shorter wavelengths mean it is moving toward us, and the size of the shift gives the speed. (3) If we know how much light the object really gives off, its dimness tells us how far away it is, because the light spreads over a sphere of area 4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>.

answer.html: The light from a nebula or galaxy tells us what it is made of (spectral line wavelengths), how fast it moves toward or away from us (Doppler shift), and roughly how far away it is (apparent brightness).

check.html: Each statement uses an idea from this module: spectra, the Doppler shift, and the inverse-square law.

items.title: CER (Claim, Evidence, Reasoning) for Module 15

body.html: Write a claim about what light from a distant galaxy reveals, supported by evidence and reasoning.
Light from a distant galaxy tells us its composition, its motion relative to us, and its distance.

(a) Visible light has wavelengths from about 400 nm to 700 nm, and a prism spreads white light into a spectrum of colors. (b) For a receding source, 𝜆<sub>𝑜𝑏𝑠</sub>−𝜆= (𝑣/ 𝑐)𝜆: a line emitted at 434 nm and seen at 440 nm in a galaxy receding at 4.20 × 10<sup>6</sup> m/s (Practice Problem 18). (c) Illuminance follows 𝐸= 𝑃/ (4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>), so a lamp moved to 4 times the distance gives 1 / 16 of the illuminance (Practice Problem 1). (d) Light travels at the finite speed 𝑐, so light from distant objects shows them as they were in the past.

Each element has its own set of wavelengths, so matching lines identifies the elements. A uniform shift of all lines is the Doppler effect, which depends only on relative velocity, so the size of the shift gives the speed and its direction (longer or shorter) gives away or toward. Light spreads over a sphere of area 4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>, so comparing apparent brightness with actual brightness gives distance.

answer.html: (Sample CER written here; student wording may vary.) The evidence supports the claim that galaxy light reveals composition, motion, and distance.

check.html: The claim is backed by at least one quantitative piece of evidence from each lesson.

items.title: Ask Questions (driving question board)

body.html: Add at least three new questions about light from space to the class driving question board.
Good questions ask how or why something about light works, and can be investigated with measurements.

answer.html: Sample questions: How can two different gases both produce a red color but have different spectral lines? How large a wavelength shift can a telescope measure? Does a galaxy look dimmer because it is far away or because it is intrinsically faint? What happens to the light's color if a source moves sideways instead of toward us? (Student questions will vary.)

check.html: Each question can be tied to wavelength, brightness, or motion, the main ideas of the module.

items.title: Collect Evidence, Revisit the Encounter the Phenomenon Question (Lesson 1 and Lesson 2 prompts)

body.html: After each lesson, record evidence in a journal and say which ideas from the lesson help answer the question about what light from a faraway object tells us.
Lesson 1 deals with how bright light looks and how fast it travels; Lesson 2 deals with light as a wave, color, and the Doppler shift.

answer.html: Lesson 1 contributes the inverse-square law for illuminance (dimmer means farther) and the finite speed of light (we see distant objects as they were in the past). Lesson 2 contributes the wave model, the link between color and wavelength, and the Doppler shift (motion toward or away, and composition from spectral lines). (Student journal entries will vary.)

check.html: Matches the CER evidence above.

items.title: Figure 1 caption question: A photograph shows sunbeams streaming through a gap in a cloud over a lake as sharp, straight rays. Explain how this picture shows the wave properties of light.

body.html: Straight, sharp-edged beams of light are seen above a lake. Decide what wave idea explains them.
The straight-line (ray) model describes a wave well when the wavelength is tiny compared with the size of the opening it passes through.

The wavelength of light (about 400 to 700 nm) is far smaller than a gap in the clouds (many meters). Diffraction, the bending of waves around edges, is therefore extremely slight, so the light looks like straight rays. The beams are visible because water droplets and haze scatter some light toward our eyes, and the slightly soft edges of each beam are the small wave effect.

answer.html: The photo mostly shows the ray (straight-line) behavior of light. It is consistent with the wave model because the wavelength is much smaller than the openings, so diffraction is tiny and the light appears to travel in straight lines; the slightly fuzzy beam edges are the small wave effect.

check.html: Sharp edges appear when the wavelength is much less than the opening size, as Huygens' principle predicts.

items.title: Recognize (Figure 3): What, if anything, could you see in a sealed, windowless closet with the lights off and no glowing objects?

body.html: A closet with no luminous source. What is visible?
Illuminated objects are seen only because they reflect light from a luminous source into the eye.
With no luminous source there is no light to reflect, so no light reaches the eyes.

answer.html: Nothing would be visible, because no light would be emitted or reflected toward your eyes.

check.html: Consistent with the idea that seeing requires light entering the eye.

items.title: Get It? (Light and matter): Why can you see through a clear glass window and also see the faint reflection of your own face in it?

body.html: Explain both the see-through view and the reflection for a transparent material.
A transparent medium transmits most light but reflects a small part.

Most light passes through the glass, so you see the scene outside. A small fraction reflects from the glass surfaces back into your eyes, so you also see your reflection, especially when it is darker outside than inside.

answer.html: Glass transmits most of the light (so you see outside) and reflects a little (so you see your reflection and the glass itself).

check.html: Same reasoning as seeing both the contents and the surface of a transparent object.

items.title: Get It? (Illuminance): Define illuminance and state its units.

body.html: A definition and units for 𝐸.
Illuminance is how much luminous flux lands on each square meter of a surface, 𝐸= 𝑃/ 𝐴.
Flux is measured in lumens (lm) and area in square meters, so the unit is lm/m², which is given the name lux.

answer.html: Illuminance 𝐸 is the luminous flux per unit area falling on a surface. Its unit is the lux (lx), where 1 lx = 1 lm/m<sup>2</sup>.

check.html: For a point source, 𝐸= 𝑃/ (4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>) has units lm/m², the same.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts (Systems and System Models): Write a paragraph on how a simplified model, such as a point source in the middle of a sphere, helps us predict how bright a light looks. Name the system and its boundary.

body.html: A short paragraph that names the system, its boundary, a mathematical relationship, and a limitation.
A model chooses a system, ignores what is outside it, and uses simplifying assumptions so mathematics can be applied.

answer.html: To predict how bright a streetlight appears, a scientist can model it as a small point source at the center of an imaginary sphere. The system is the lamp plus the light it emits; the boundary is the surface of the sphere, since all of the light must pass through it. The sphere has area 4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>, so the model predicts 𝐸= 𝑃/ (4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>), an inverse-square relationship. The model assumes a small source and light striking the surface straight on, so it is less accurate for a long fluorescent tube, for a lamp with a reflector that sends light mostly in one direction, or for a lamp very close to the surface. Ole Roemer used another model: the system of Earth, Jupiter, and Io, with the planetary orbits as the boundary, to estimate the speed of light.

check.html: Names the system, the boundary, a mathematical relationship, and a limitation.

items.title: Get It? (Luminous intensity): Explain what luminous intensity measures and how it is related to illuminance.

body.html: The meaning of luminous intensity (in candelas) and its link to 𝐸.
𝐼= 𝑃/ (4𝜋), and for a point source 𝐸= 𝑃/ (4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>) = 𝐼/ 𝑟<sup>2</sup>.
Intensity is the flux sent into each unit of solid angle (per 4𝜋 of a complete sphere). Dividing it by the distance squared gives the flux per square meter at that distance.

answer.html: Luminous intensity (in candelas) is the luminous flux a point source sends out per 4𝜋 of a full sphere, which is the flux landing on 1 m<sup>2</sup> of the inside of a sphere of radius 1 m. Illuminance is the intensity divided by the distance squared, 𝐸= 𝐼/ 𝑟<sup>2</sup>, so it is directly proportional to intensity and inversely proportional to 𝑟<sup>2</sup>.

check.html: For 𝑃= 1600 lm: 𝐼= 1600 / (4𝜋) = 127 cd and 𝐸= 127 lx at 1 m, matching 𝐸= 𝑃/ (4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>).

items.title: Check Your Progress 8 (Light): A laser pointer beam crosses a dusty room. Describe two observations that show light travels in straight lines.

body.html: Straight-line travel (the ray model) explains sharp beams and shadows.

answer.html: (1) The laser beam is a straight line in the dusty air, and you can sight along it with a ruler. (2) A fence post casts a shadow with the same shape as the post, and the edges of the shadow line up with straight lines drawn from the lamp past the post's edges. (Sample evidence; any similar observations are acceptable.)

check.html: Both are consistent with the ray model of light.

items.title: Check Your Progress 9 (Light properties): Why might you choose frosted (translucent) glass for a bathroom window, and an opaque cover for a darkroom door?

body.html: Translucent materials transmit light but scatter it so no clear image forms; opaque materials transmit no light.

answer.html: Frosted glass lets daylight in while blurring the view, so the room is lit but people cannot see in clearly. An opaque cover blocks all the light, so a darkroom (or a sleeping room) stays dark.

check.html: Matches the definitions: translucent transmits but gives no clear image; opaque absorbs or reflects all the light.

items.title: Check Your Progress 10 (Illuminance): Does one lightbulb at distance 𝑟 provide more or less illuminance than three identical bulbs at twice the distance?

Illuminance adds for several sources and follows 𝐸= 𝑃/ (4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>).

answer.html: One bulb at 𝑟 gives more illuminance: the three bulbs at 2𝑟 give only 3 / 4 as much.

check.html: Doubling the distance cuts 𝐸 to 1/4 and tripling the number of bulbs multiplies it by 3, so the net is 3 / 4.

items.title: Check Your Progress 15 (Critical thinking): A student repeats Roemer's idea for a smaller orbit. Light is timed crossing the diameter of Mercury's orbit, 1.16 × 1011 m, in 6.50 min. Find the speed of light from these data. Is the method accurate? Why might a historical first attempt have been less accurate?

body.html: Speed = distance/time.

answer.html: 𝑐≈2.97 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s. Yes, the method appears accurate, because this is within about 0.8% of the accepted value 2.998 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s. An early attempt could be off because the timing was crude (no precise clocks, and the start and end of an eclipse are hard to judge) and the orbit size was not well known, not because the idea was flawed.

items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon: What does the light from a distant star or supernova tell us about it?

body.html: Light carries information in its wavelength (color) and its brightness. The Doppler shift tells us motion, spectral lines tell us composition, and illuminance tells us distance.

(1) A star's spectrum has lines at wavelengths that match the lines of elements measured in a lab on Earth, so we can identify what the star is made of. (2) If those lines are shifted to longer wavelengths (red shift) the object moves away from us; if shifted shorter (blue shift) it moves toward us, with 𝛥𝜆= ± (𝑣/ 𝑐)𝜆 giving the speed. (3) Because illuminance falls as 𝐸= 𝑃/ (4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>), a star's apparent brightness, combined with a known luminous flux, tells us how far away it is.

answer.html: Light from a distant star or supernova tells us what it is made of (spectral line wavelengths), how fast it moves toward or away from us (Doppler shift), and, from its apparent brightness, how far away it is.

check.html: Each statement uses an equation or idea from this module (spectra, Doppler shift, inverse-square law).

items.title: CER (Claim, Evidence, Reasoning) for Module 15

body.html: Light from a distant star or supernova tells us its composition, its motion relative to us, and its distance.

(a) Light has wavelengths from about 400 nm to 700 nm and each color has its own wavelength; a prism spreads white light into a spectrum. (b) 𝜆<sub>𝑜𝑏𝑠</sub>−𝜆= ± (𝑣/ 𝑐)𝜆: a hydrogen line at 486 nm seen at 497 nm in a galaxy receding at 6.55 × 10<sup>6</sup> m/s (Practice Problem 18). (c) Illuminance follows 𝐸= 𝑃/ (4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>), so a source 3 times farther gives 1/9 the illuminance (Practice Problem 1). (d) Light travels at a finite speed, so light from distant objects shows them as they were in the past.

Each element emits specific wavelengths, so matching lines identifies the star's elements. A uniform shift of all lines is the Doppler effect, which depends only on relative velocity, so the size of the shift gives the speed and its direction (red or blue) gives toward or away. Brightness spreads over a sphere of area 4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>, so comparing apparent and actual brightness gives distance.

answer.html: (Sample CER written here; student wording may vary.) The evidence supports the claim that starlight reveals composition, motion, and distance.

check.html: The claim is supported by at least one quantitative piece of evidence from each lesson.

items.title: Figure 1 caption question: Explain how this photo demonstrates the wave properties of light.

body.html: The photo shows beams of light crossing a forest as straight lines. That mainly shows the ray model (straight-line travel), which is the simplest way to describe a wave when the wavelength is tiny compared with the objects it meets (tree branches, gaps).

Because the wavelength of light (about 400–700 nm) is far smaller than the gaps between branches, diffraction is very slight, so the beams look straight with fairly sharp edges. The beams are visible because dust and mist scatter some of the light toward our eyes, and shadows have fuzzy edges because the wave bends slightly at edges.

answer.html: The photo mostly shows the ray (straight-line) behavior of light. It is consistent with the wave model because the wavelength is much smaller than the openings, so bending (diffraction) is tiny and the light appears to travel in straight lines; the slightly soft beam edges are the small wave effect.

check.html: The explanation is consistent with Huygens' principle: sharp edges appear when the wavelength is much less than the gap size.

items.title: Recognize (Figure 3): What, if anything, would be visible if the room had no luminous source?

body.html: Illuminated objects are seen only by reflecting light from a luminous source into the eye.
With no luminous source there is no light to reflect, so nothing reaches the eyes.

answer.html: Nothing would be visible, because no light would be emitted or reflected.

check.html: Matches the text: "in a room with no light, it would be impossible to see anything."

items.title: Get It? (Light and matter): Why can you see a fish through a glass fishbowl and also see the glass of the bowl?

body.html: A transparent medium transmits most light but reflects a small part.
Most light passes through the glass, so you see the fish. Some light is reflected from the glass surfaces into your eyes, so you also see the bowl.

answer.html: Glass transmits most light (so the fish is visible) and reflects a little (so the glass itself is visible).

check.html: Same reasoning as the transparent candle holder in Figure 4.

items.title: Get It? (Illuminance): Define illuminance and state its units.

answer.html: Illuminance 𝐸 is the luminous flux falling on a given surface area. It is measured in lux (lx), where 1 lx = 1 lm/m<sup>2</sup>.

check.html: Consistent with 𝐸= 𝑃/ (4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>), where 𝑃 is in lm and area in m².

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts (Systems and System Models): Write a paragraph on how mathematical models were used in the study of light, including the system and system boundaries.

body.html: A model chooses a system, ignores what is outside it, and uses simplifying assumptions so mathematics can be applied.

answer.html: Scientists modeled light with rays that travel in straight lines until they meet a boundary. For illuminance they chose as the system a point source of light at the center of an imaginary sphere; the sphere's surface was the system boundary, because all of the source's light passes through it. Using the surface area of the sphere, 4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>, they modeled illuminance as 𝐸= 𝑃/ (4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>), an inverse-square relationship. The model assumes a small point source and light striking the surface perpendicularly, so it is less accurate for long fluorescent tubes or for lamps very close to a surface. Roemer similarly modeled the system of Earth, Jupiter, and Io (the boundary being their orbits) to find the speed of light.

check.html: Names the system, boundary, mathematical relationship, and a limitation.

items.title: Get It? (Luminous intensity): Describe what luminous intensity measures and its relationship to illuminance.

answer.html: Luminous intensity (in candelas) is the luminous flux per 4𝜋 of a point source, that is, the flux falling on 1 m<sup>2</sup> of the inside of a 1-m-radius sphere. Illuminance is the intensity divided by the distance squared, 𝐸= 𝐼/ 𝑟<sup>2</sup>, so it is directly proportional to the intensity and inversely proportional to 𝑟<sup>2</sup>.

check.html: For 𝑃= 1750 lm: 𝐼= 139 cd, and 𝐸= 139 / (1 m)<sup>2</sup> = 139 lx at 1 m, matching the text.

items.title: Practice Problem 1: A lamp is moved from 30 cm to 90 cm above a book. Compare the illumination before and after.

body.html: 𝑟<sub>1</sub> = 30 cm, 𝑟<sub>2</sub> = 90 cm; compare 𝐸<sub>2</sub> to 𝐸<sub>1</sub>.
The same lamp (same 𝑃) gives 𝐸∝1 / 𝑟<sup>2</sup> (inverse-square law).
The distance became 3 times larger, so the illumination is 1 / 3<sup>2</sup> = 1 / 9 as great.

answer.html: The illumination after the move is 1 / 9 of the illumination before (about 0.11 times as much).

items.title: Check Your Progress 8 (Light): What evidence have you observed that light travels in a straight line?

answer.html: Sunbeams through a window or trees, or a flashlight beam in dusty air, travel as straight lines; sharp shadows have the shape of the object blocking the light; and you cannot see around a corner or through a hole in a bent tube. (Sample evidence; any similar observations are acceptable.)

check.html: All are consistent with the ray model.

items.title: Check Your Progress 9 (Light properties): Why might you choose a window shade that is translucent? Opaque?

answer.html: A translucent shade lets light in (to light the room) but blurs images, so people cannot see in clearly and you keep privacy by day. An opaque shade blocks the light (and the view), good for sleeping, darkening a room for a presentation, or privacy at night.

check.html: Matches the definitions: translucent transmits but does not form clear images; opaque absorbs/reflects all.

items.title: Check Your Progress 10 (Illuminance): Does one lightbulb provide more or less illuminance than two identical bulbs at twice the distance?

body.html: One bulb at distance 𝑟 versus two identical bulbs (flux 𝑃 each) at distance 2𝑟.
Illuminance adds for several sources and follows 𝐸= 𝑃/ (4𝜋𝑟<sup>2</sup>).

answer.html: One bulb at 𝑟 gives more illuminance: twice as much as two identical bulbs at 2𝑟 (which give half of 𝐸<sub>1</sub>).

check.html: Doubling the distance cuts 𝐸 to 1/4, and doubling the number of bulbs only doubles it, so the net is 1/2.
